# SNMPv1, SNMPv2c & Encrypted SNMPv3 (`docs/l7_snmp.md`)

[**Use Cases**](#snmp-testing-and-security-use-cases) • [**How It Works**](#what-frameassembly-handles-for-you) • [**Keywords & Modifiers**](#snmp-keywords-and-modifiers) • [**All 9 VarBind Types & OIDs**](#varbind-types-and-common-mib-oids) • [**Wireshark Decryption**](#decrypting-and-replaying-snmpv3-captures)

## Why Use FrameAssembly for SNMP?

Simulating SNMP traffic—especially encrypted **SNMPv3 `authPriv` traps**—is normally way harder than whatever monitoring rule you are actually trying to test.

If you want to verify that **Zabbix**, **Checkmk**, **LibreNMS**, **PRTG**, **SolarWinds**, **Datadog**, or `snmptrapd` actually pages the on-call engineer when a core uplink dies, your usual options are grim -> configure an SNMP agent, hunt down broken vendor MIB dependencies, match hex EngineIDs and localized keys, and physically yank a patch cord out of a switch just to watch a dashboard turn red :)

With **FrameAssembly**, you describe the poll, walk, `set`, or encrypted trap in a few lines of `.fasm` code, compile a `.pcap` file without MIB dependencies, and fire it at your collector or IDS with **`tcpreplay`**:

```frameassembly
host core_sw { ip 10.10.1.2  mac 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:01 }
host zabbix  { ip 10.10.1.50 mac 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:50 }

flow link_down_alert(sw, nms) {
    // SNMPv2c linkDown trap (sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0 are added automatically)
    sw -> nms snmp2 trap community "public" sysuptime 432000 oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.3 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.1 string "Gi0/1" varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.1 int 2 wait 5ms

    // Encrypted SNMPv3 authPriv trap (SHA-256 + AES-128) on VLAN 100
    sw -> nms vlan 100 snmp3 trap user "netops" engineid "80001f8801" engineboots 5 enginetime 3600 auth sha256 "AuthPass123!" priv aes "PrivPass123!" sysuptime 432005 oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.3 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.1 int 2
}

compile { link_down_alert(core_sw, zabbix) }
```

```console
$ frameassembly show snmp_alert.fasm
$ frameassembly snmp_alert.fasm snmp_alert.pcap && sudo tcpreplay -i eth0 snmp_alert.pcap
```

## SNMP Testing and Security Use Cases

### 1. Test Encrypted `snmp3` `authPriv` Traps & `inform` Alerts Without Touching Live Gear
Getting SNMPv3 `authPriv` traps working between a router and an NMS is notorious for silent packet drops whenever an `engineid`, `engineboots` counter, `enginetime` window, or SHA-2/AES key doesn't line up. Instead of fighting `snmptrap` CLI flags or rebooting lab gear, pass plain passphrases in `.fasm` code—FrameAssembly derives the localized keys, encrypts the payload, signs the packet, and handles acknowledged `inform` -> `response` handshakes out of the box:

```frameassembly
host core_rtr { ip 10.151.0.1   mac 00:25:90:51:00:01 }
host nms_srv  { ip 10.151.0.250 mac 00:25:90:51:00:fa }

flow snmpv3_alerts(rtr, nms) {
    // Encrypted SNMPv3 TRAP (SHA-256 + AES-128) reporting a 100G uplink down
    rtr -> nms dscp 16 snmp3 trap user "ops_v3" engineid "80001f8880510001" engineboots 30 enginetime 400000 contextname "core-fabric" auth sha256 "ProdAuthPass2026!" priv aes "ProdPrivPass2026!" reqid 9701 sysuptime 40000000 oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.3 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.1.10 string "HundredGigE0/0/0/10" varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.10 int 2 wait 5ms

    // Guaranteed-delivery SNMPv3 INFORM + NMS RESPONSE on UDP 162 (SHA-512 + AES-128)
    rtr -> nms dscp 16 snmp3 inform dstport 162 user "ops_v3" engineid "80001f8880510001" engineboots 30 enginetime 400001 contextname "core-fabric" auth sha512 "HighSecSha512!" priv aes "HighSecAes128!" reqid 9702 sysuptime 40000100 oid 1.3.6.1.2.1.15.7.2 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.15.3.1.2.198.51.100.2 int 1 wait 2ms
    rtr <- nms dscp 16 snmp3 response user "ops_v3" engineid "80001f8880510001" engineboots 30 enginetime 400001 contextname "core-fabric" auth sha512 "HighSecSha512!" priv aes "HighSecAes128!" reqid 9702 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.15.3.1.2.198.51.100.2 int 1
}

compile { snmpv3_alerts(core_rtr, nms_srv) }
```

### 2. Stress-Test Collector Queues & Alert Deduplication (Trap Bursts & Link Flaps)
Finding out *during* a real fiber cut that a single flapping port sends 500 Slack alerts or chokes your trap daemon is bad timing. Invoke a `linkDown` / `linkUp` flow back-to-back inside `compile` to verify alert throttling and deduplication before production finds out for you:

```frameassembly
host flapping_sw { ip 10.125.0.10  mac 00:1c:73:25:00:10 }
host trap_sink   { ip 10.125.0.250 mac 00:1c:73:25:00:fa }

flow link_flap_cycle(sw, sink) {
    sw -> sink snmp2 trap community "noc_traps" reqid 6001 sysuptime 300100 oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.3 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.10 string "Ethernet10" varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.10 int 2 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.5.10 gauge32 0 wait 50ms
    sw -> sink snmp2 trap community "noc_traps" reqid 6002 sysuptime 300105 oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.4 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.10 string "Ethernet10" varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.10 int 1 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.5.10 gauge32 1000000000 wait 50ms
}

compile {
    link_flap_cycle(flapping_sw, trap_sink)
    link_flap_cycle(flapping_sw, trap_sink)
    link_flap_cycle(flapping_sw, trap_sink)
}
```

### 3. Simulate 400G `counter64` `getbulk` Polls, Optical Sensors & Multi-VRF Contexts
Testing custom NMS templates, Prometheus `snmp_exporter` parsers, 64-bit interface counter wraps, negative optical `dBm` readings, or per-VRF routing table queries usually requires physical spine switches and MPLS PE routers. Here you can script the exact `getbulk` / `get` and `response` packets—exercising all 9 `varbind` types—in one flow:

```frameassembly
host poller    { ip 10.156.0.10 mac 00:1b:54:56:00:10 }
host pe_router { ip 10.156.0.1  mac 00:1b:54:56:00:01 }

flow poll_counters_and_vrfs(nms, pe) {
    // SNMPv2c GETBULK: fetch 1 scalar (sysUpTime.0) + repeating 400G Counter64 & optical dBm rows
    nms -> pe snmp2 getbulk community "telemetry_ro" reqid 7001 nonrepeaters 1 maxrepetitions 10 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 null varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6 null wait 2ms
    nms <- pe snmp2 response community "telemetry_ro" reqid 7001 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 timeticks 8640000 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0 oidval 1.3.6.1.4.1.30065.1.3011 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.1.1 string "Ethernet1/1" varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.1 counter64 2199023255552 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.14.1 counter32 0 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.15.1 gauge32 400000 varbind 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.91.1.1.1.1.4.1 int -7 wait 5ms

    // SNMPv3 multi-tenant VRF poll isolated via contextname "vrf-pci"
    nms -> pe snmp3 get user "vrf_auditor" engineid "800000090300001b54560001" engineboots 10 enginetime 80000 contextname "vrf-pci" auth sha256 "VrfAuthKey!" priv aes "VrfPrivKey!" reqid 7002 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.21.1.7.0.0.0.0 null wait 2ms
    nms <- pe snmp3 response user "vrf_auditor" engineid "800000090300001b54560001" engineboots 10 enginetime 80000 contextname "vrf-pci" auth sha256 "VrfAuthKey!" priv aes "VrfPrivKey!" reqid 7002 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.21.1.7.0.0.0.0 ipval 172.31.254.1
}

compile { poll_counters_and_vrfs(poller, pe_router) }
```

### 4. Pentesting, Rogue `set` Detection & IDS Rule Validation (Suricata, Zeek, SIEM)
Leftover `"public"` and `"private"` community strings are still an internal pentester's best friend. Build zero-noise captures to verify that **Suricata**, **Zeek**, or your SIEM flags unauthenticated SNMPv3 EngineID discovery probes, unauthorized `set` requests shutting down switch ports (`ifAdminStatus = 2`), and resulting `authenticationFailure` traps:

```frameassembly
host rogue_scanner { ip 192.168.66.13 mac 00:0c:29:66:00:13 }
host access_sw     { ip 192.168.66.1  mac 00:1c:73:66:00:01 }
host secops_siem   { ip 10.104.0.99   mac 00:19:56:00:01:99 }

flow snmp_pentest_and_detection(attacker, sw, siem) {
    // 1. Unauthenticated SNMPv3 EngineID discovery probe
    attacker -> sw snmp3 get user "" engineid "0000000000" engineboots 0 enginetime 0 reqid 8001 wait 2ms
    attacker <- sw snmp3 response user "" engineid "80001f8880660001" engineboots 4 enginetime 9200 reqid 8001 varbind 1.3.6.1.6.3.15.1.1.4.0 counter32 1 wait 5ms

    // 2. Rogue SNMPv2c SET using default "private" write community to admin-down port 24
    attacker -> sw snmp2 set community "private" reqid 8002 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.24 int 2 wait 2ms
    attacker <- sw snmp2 response community "private" reqid 8002 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.24 int 2 wait 5ms

    // 3. Switch alerts SecOps with an SNMPv1 authenticationFailure trap (gentrap 4)
    sw -> siem snmp1 trap community "sec_trap" enterprise 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.1 agentip 192.168.66.1 gentrap 4 spectrap 0 sysuptime 543210 varbind 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.2.1.5.0 ipval 192.168.66.13 varbind 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.2.1.6.0 string "bad_community_attempt"
}

compile { snmp_pentest_and_detection(rogue_scanner, access_sw, secops_siem) }
```

```console
$ frameassembly snmp_ids.fasm snmp_ids.pcap && suricata -r snmp_ids.pcap -k none
```

### 5. Legacy `snmp1` UPS/Printer Hardware, `md5`/`des` & Carrier `qinq` + `mpls`
Every network has that one ancient UPS management card, laser printer, or branch CPE that only speaks `snmp1` (`gentrap` / `spectrap`) or legacy `snmp3` `md5` + `des`—sometimes riding across a carrier `qinq` + `mpls` backhaul or IPv6 management network:

```frameassembly
host ups_card     { ip 10.145.40.5   mac 00:1a:2b:91:40:05 }
host noc_srv      { ip 10.145.40.100 mac 00:1a:2b:91:40:64 }
host v6_agent     { ip 2001:db8:3::1 }
host v6_collector { ip 2001:db8:3::2 }

flow legacy_and_carrier_snmp(agent, nms) {
    // SNMPv1 enterprise-specific UPS "on battery" trap (gentrap 6, spectrap 1)
    agent -> nms snmp1 trap community "ups_traps" enterprise 1.3.6.1.2.1.33.2 agentip 10.145.40.5 gentrap 6 spectrap 1 sysuptime 9912400 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.33.1.2.3.0 int 28 wait 5ms

    // Legacy SNMPv3 MD5 + DES trap inside Carrier QinQ (800/162) and MPLS label 7300
    agent -> nms qinq 800 innervlan 162 mpls 7300 snmp3 trap user "legacy_ups" engineid "80001f8880aa11bb22" engineboots 4 enginetime 12000 auth md5 "LegacyMd5Key!" priv des "LegacyDesKey!" oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.3 sysuptime 1200000 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.2.3 string "FastEthernet0/3"
}

flow ipv6_snmp_traps(a6, n6) {
    // Over IPv6, SNMPv1 automatically sets the 4-byte agent-addr field to 0.0.0.0 (RFC 3584)
    a6 -> n6 snmp1 trap community "public" enterprise 1.3.6.1.4.1.318 gentrap 6 spectrap 5 sysuptime 90000 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 string "ups-row4-v6" wait 5ms
    a6 -> n6 snmp3 trap user "ops_v6" engineid "80001f8880660006" auth sha256 "Ipv6AuthPass!" priv aes "Ipv6PrivPass!" oid 1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.4 varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.34.1.3.2.16 ipval 2001:db8:3::1
}

compile {
    legacy_and_carrier_snmp(ups_card, noc_srv)
    ipv6_snmp_traps(v6_agent, v6_collector)
}
```

## What FrameAssembly Handles for You

* **Smart UDP `161` vs. `162` Port Routing:** Polling operations (`get`, `getnext`, `getbulk`, `set`, `response`) automatically target **UDP `161`**, while notifications (`trap`, `inform`) target **UDP `162`**. Replies on `<-` automatically flip the ports back to the sender's ephemeral port (add `dstport 162` on `inform` or `srcport 162` on its `response` so the reply comes from `162`).
* **Zero MIB Files Needed:** Forget `MIBS=+ALL` path errors. Write numeric OIDs (`1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0`, quoted or unquoted) paired with plain type names (`string`, `int`, `counter64`, `ipval`, etc.).
* **Auto-Prepended Trap Headers:** Every `snmp2` and `snmp3` `trap` or `inform` requires `sysUpTime.0` and `snmpTrapOID.0` as its first two VarBinds. FrameAssembly prepends both automatically from `sysuptime` and `oid`, then appends your `varbind` list in order.
* **Built-In SNMPv3 USM Crypto:** Pass cleartext passwords to `auth` (`md5`, `sha`, `sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`) and `priv` (`des`, `aes`). FrameAssembly localizes the keys against `engineid`, encrypts the `scopedPDU`, and signs the BER packet so Wireshark and `snmptrapd` can decrypt and verify it immediately.
* **Zero-Keyword Defaults:** Even a bare `sw -> nms snmp1`, `sw -> nms snmp2`, or `sw -> nms snmp3` compiles into a valid RFC trap on UDP `162`.

## SNMP Keywords and Modifiers

| Version | Keyword | Default Ports | Auth / Crypto | Supported Operations |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **SNMPv1** | `snmp1` | `161` (Poll), `162` (Trap) | `community "<str>"` | `get`, `getnext`, `set`, `response`, `trap` |
| **SNMPv2c** | `snmp2` | `161` (Poll), `162` (Trap/Inform) | `community "<str>"` | `get`, `getnext`, `getbulk`, `set`, `response`, `trap`, `inform` |
| **SNMPv3** | `snmp3` | `161` (Poll), `162` (Trap/Inform) | `noAuthNoPriv`, `authNoPriv`, `authPriv` | `get`, `getnext`, `getbulk`, `set`, `response`, `trap`, `inform` |

### Shared & Version-Specific Modifiers

| Modifier | Applies To | Default | What It Does |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `community "<str>"` | `snmp1`, `snmp2` | `"public"` | Cleartext community string (`"public"`, `"private"`, etc.) |
| `reqid <u32>` | `snmp1`, `snmp2`, `snmp3` | `1` | Request/Message ID matching a `response` to its request or `inform` |
| `sysuptime <ticks>` | `snmp1`, `snmp2`, `snmp3` | `0` | Agent uptime in `1/100`s ticks (`Trap-PDU` timestamp in v1; `sysUpTime.0` in v2c/v3) |
| `oid <oid>` | `snmp1`, `snmp2`, `snmp3` | `linkDown` (v2c/v3) | Notification OID for `trap`/`inform` (or shorthand single-OID `null` query on `get`) |
| `nonrepeaters <n>` | `snmp2`, `snmp3` | `0` | First `<n>` scalar OIDs in a `getbulk` request fetched only once |
| `maxrepetitions <m>` | `snmp2`, `snmp3` | `10` | Max table rows fetched per remaining OID in a `getbulk` request |
| `enterprise <oid>` | `snmp1` | `1.3.6.1.4.1` | Vendor enterprise OID in an SNMPv1 `Trap-PDU` |
| `agentip <ipv4>` | `snmp1` | Sender IPv4 (`0.0.0.0` on v6) | Overrides inner `agent-addr` (useful when simulating an SNMP trap proxy/concentrator) |
| `gentrap <0..6>` | `snmp1` | `6` (or auto from `oid`) | `0` coldStart, `1` warmStart, `2` linkDown, `3` linkUp, `4` authFailure, `5` egpNeighborLoss, `6` enterpriseSpecific |
| `spectrap <u32>` | `snmp1` | `0` (`0..5`) / `1` (`6`) | Vendor-specific trap sub-code when `gentrap` is `6` |
| `user "<name>"` | `snmp3` | `"admin"` | USM username (`""` for EngineID discovery probes) |
| `engineid "<hex>"` | `snmp3` | `"8000000001"` | Even-length hex EngineID string (e.g., `"80001f8880510001"`) |
| `engineboots <u32>` | `snmp3` | `0` | Engine reboot counter (used in anti-replay & AES-128 IV) |
| `enginetime <u32>` | `snmp3` | `0` | Seconds since last engine boot (used in anti-replay & AES-128 IV) |
| `contextname "<str>"`| `snmp3` | `""` | VRF, bridge-domain, or per-VLAN MIB context name (e.g., `"vrf-pci"`) |
| `auth <alg> "<pass>"`| `snmp3` | None (`noAuth`) | Signs packet with unquoted `md5`, `sha`, `sha256`, `sha384`, or `sha512` + passphrase |
| `priv <alg> "<pass>"`| `snmp3` | None (`noPriv`) | Encrypts `scopedPDU` with unquoted `des` or `aes` + passphrase (requires `auth`) |

> **Quick Syntax Check:** Keep `auth` and `priv` algorithm names **unquoted**, and put quotes around the password -> `auth sha256 "MyAuthPass!" priv aes "MyPrivPass!"` (never `auth "sha256"`). Also note that SNMPv3 forbids encryption without authentication (`priv` always requires `auth`), and `counter64` / `getbulk` / `inform` are `snmp2` and `snmp3` only.

## VarBind Types and Common MIB OIDs

Chain as many `varbind <oid> <type> [value]` entries onto a single statement as you want:

| Type Keyword | Example | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `null` / `nullval` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 null` | Empty placeholder used in `get`, `getnext`, and `getbulk` requests |
| `string "<text>"` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0 string "core-sw"` | Hostnames, interface names, serial numbers, and status messages |
| `int <-2B..2B>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.8.1 int 2` | Signed 32-bit integer (`1`=up, `2`=down, or negative values like `-18` dBm / `-15` °C) |
| `timeticks <u32>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0 timeticks 8640000` | Elapsed time in `1/100`s centiseconds (`8640000` = 24 hours) |
| `ipval <ip>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.20.1.1.10.0.0.1 ipval 10.0.0.1` | Accepts both IPv4 (`IpAddress`) and IPv6 (`2001:db8::1` 16-byte `InetAddress`) |
| `oidval <oid>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0 oidval 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.1.1` | Value that points to another OID (such as `sysObjectID.0`) |
| `counter32 <u32>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.1 counter32 459012` | Wrapping 32-bit packet/byte/error counter |
| `gauge32 <u32>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.5.1 gauge32 1000000000` | Non-wrapping 32-bit gauge (link speed, CPU %, PoE watts, queue depth) |
| `counter64 <u64>` | `varbind 1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.1 counter64 98765432100` | 64-bit high-speed counter (`ifHCInOctets` / `ifHCOutOctets`; `snmp2` & `snmp3` only) |

### Handy MIB-II & Standard Trap OIDs (So You Don't Have to Google Them)

| Object / Trap | OID | Typical Type | Common Values |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `sysDescr.0` / `sysObjectID.0` | `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0` / `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0` | `string` / `oidval` | OS version banner / vendor model OID |
| `sysUpTime.0` | `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0` | `timeticks` | Uptime in hundredths of a second |
| `sysContact.0` / `sysName.0` / `sysLocation.0` | `1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0` / `.5.0` / `.6.0` | `string` | Admin email, hostname, rack location |
| `ifIndex.<n>` / `ifDescr.<n>` | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.1.<n>` / `.2.<n>` | `int` / `string` | Port index (`1`, `2`) / name (`"Gi0/1"`) |
| `ifAdminStatus.<n>` / `ifOperStatus.<n>` | `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.7.<n>` / `.8.<n>` | `int` | `1` = up, `2` = down, `3` = testing |
| `ifHCInOctets.<n>` / `ifHCOutOctets.<n>` | `1.3.6.1.2.1.31.1.1.1.6.<n>` / `.10.<n>` | `counter64` | 64-bit inbound / outbound byte counters |
| `coldStart` / `warmStart` | `1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.1` / `1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.2` | Trap `oid` | Device rebooted / SNMP agent restarted |
| `linkDown` / `linkUp` | `1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.3` / `1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.4` | Trap `oid` | Interface went down / came back up |
| `authenticationFailure` | `1.3.6.1.6.3.1.1.5.5` | Trap `oid` | Bad community string or unauthorized poll |

## Decrypting and Replaying SNMPv3 Captures

### Decrypt `snmp3` in `tshark` (One-Liner)
```bash
tshark -r snmp_alert.pcap \
  -o 'uat:snmp_users:"80001f8801","netops","SHA2-256","AuthPass123!","AES","PrivPass123!"' \
  -V
```

### Decrypt `snmp3` in the Wireshark GUI
Open **Edit -> Preferences -> Protocols -> SNMP -> Users Table -> Edit...**, add your **Engine ID** (`80001f8801`, or leave blank to match all), **Username** (`netops`), **Auth model** (`SHA2-256`, `SHA2-512`, `SHA2-384`, `SHA1`, or `MD5`), **Auth password**, **Priv protocol** (`AES` or `DES`), and **Priv password**. Wireshark immediately unlocks the `encryptedPDU` and shows `[Authentication OK]`.

### Replay into a Live Collector (`tcpreplay`) or Reverse Existing SNMP Captures (`frameassembly reverse`)
```bash
# Replay honoring your .fasm wait intervals
sudo tcpreplay -i eth0 snmp_alert.pcap

# Blast traps at wire speed to benchmark collector throughput
sudo tcpreplay -i eth0 --topspeed snmp_alert.pcap

# Reverse an existing SNMP .pcap / .pcapng capture into .fasm code (defaults to <input_stem>.fasm)
frameassembly reverse snmp_walk.pcap snmp_walk.fasm
```

When reversing an SNMP capture with `frameassembly reverse`, cleartext `snmp1`, `snmp2`, and `snmp3` (`noAuthNoPriv`) packets decompile directly into `snmp1` / `snmp2` / `snmp3` statements with `varbind` entries. Encrypted `snmp3` `authPriv` (or keyed `authNoPriv`) packets are not decrypted; `frameassembly reverse` keeps them as `udp` statements with `hexpayload` so recompiling preserves the exact wire bytes.

# Layer 7 — Core Infrastructure, Time, AAA & Flow Telemetry (`docs/l7_infra_and_telemetry.md`)

[**Use Cases**](#infrastructure-and-telemetry-testing-use-cases) • [**Smart Ports & Multicast**](#what-frameassembly-handles-for-you) • [**DNS, mDNS & DHCP**](#1-naming-service-discovery-and-dhcp-dns-mdns-dhcp) • [**NTP & PTP**](#2-clock-sync-and-precision-timing-ntp-ptp) • [**RADIUS & TACACS+**](#3-aaa-access-and-cli-auditing-radius-tacacs) • [**Syslog & Flow Exports**](#4-logging-and-flow-telemetry-syslog-netflow-ipfix-sflow) • [**Inspect & Replay**](#inspecting-reversing-and-replaying-infrastructure-captures)

## Why Use FrameAssembly for Infrastructure & Telemetry?

Testing core infrastructure rules, SIEM parsers, and flow collectors usually demands an absurd amount of lab plumbing for five packets of traffic. If you want to verify that **Suricata** catches an unauthorized DNS `AXFR` zone transfer, check switch DHCP snooping, test **Cisco ISE** / **FreeRADIUS** attributes, or see if **Splunk** and **ElastiFlow** parse a BGP flap, your normal options are rough -> edit `bind` zone files, configure `kea-dhcp` scopes, buy a four-figure IEEE 1588 PTP grandmaster clock, or yank a fiber out of a core router just to generate one syslog line and hope nobody notices :)

With **FrameAssembly**, you write the query, lease, AAA exchange, or flow record in a few lines of `.fasm` code, compile a `.pcap` file without running lab daemons, and feed it straight into **`tcpreplay`**, **Wireshark** / **`tshark`**, **Suricata**, or **Zeek**:

```frameassembly
host core_rtr { ip 10.250.0.1   mac 00:1c:73:fa:00:01 }
host sec_ops  { ip 10.250.0.100 mac 00:50:56:fa:00:64 }

flow noc_quick_check(rtr, col) {
    // Blocked C2 DNS lookup (RCODE 5 = REFUSED) + Syslog alert + IPFIX flow export
    rtr -> col dns query txid 0x4401 qname "c2-beacon.bad-domain.test" qtype "a" wait 1ms
    rtr <- col dns response txid 0x4401 qname "c2-beacon.bad-domain.test" qtype "a" rcode 5 wait 2ms
    rtr -> col syslog facility 16 severity 2 hostname "core-rtr-01" app "bgpd" msgid "BGP_DOWN" msg "Neighbor 198.51.100.1 Hold Timer Expired" wait 2ms
    rtr -> col ipfix domainid 4001 srcip 198.51.100.25 dstip 203.0.113.80 srcport 52400 dstport 443 proto 6 packets 15400 octets 21560000
}

compile { noc_quick_check(core_rtr, sec_ops) }
```

```console
$ frameassembly show infra_check.fasm
$ frameassembly infra_check.fasm infra_check.pcap && sudo tcpreplay -i eth0 infra_check.pcap
```

| Protocol | Keyword | Default Transport & Smart Port Routing | IPv4 & IPv6 | Primary Testing Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **DNS** | `dns` | `UDP 53` (`TCP 53` + 2B length with `transport tcp`) | Both | RPZ sinkholes (NXDOMAIN/REFUSED), AAAA/TXT/SRV, AXFR alerts |
| **Multicast DNS** | `mdns` | `UDP 5353` -> `224.0.0.251` (v4) / `ff02::fb` (v6) | Both | Bonjour/Avahi printer & IoT discovery across campus VLANs |
| **DHCPv4 / v6** | `dhcp` | `UDP 68<->67` (v4 DORA) / `UDP 546<->547` (v6 SARR) | Both | Switch DHCP snooping, rogue DHCP offers, relay ACLs |
| **NTPv4** | `ntp` | `UDP 123` | Both | Stratum-1 GPS sync, Leap Indicator alarms, Kiss-o'-Death (`RATE`) |
| **PTPv2** | `ptp` | `UDP 319` (`sync`/`delayreq`) & `320` (General) | Both | IEEE 1588v2 two-step sync, DSCP EF timing queues, EUI-64 clocks |
| **RADIUS** | `radius` | `UDP 1812` (Auth) & `UDP 1813` (Accounting) | Both | 802.1X NAC challenges, VPN Framed-IP, accounting collectors |
| **TACACS+** | `tacacs` | `TCP 49` (stateful `psh ack`) | Both | Router CLI login auth, `cmd=reload` authorization, audit logs |
| **Syslog** | `syslog` | `UDP 514` (`TCP 514` with `transport tcp`) | Both | SIEM Grok/regex parsers, facility/severity routing, reliable TCP logs |
| **NetFlow v5** | `netflow`| `UDP 2055` | Both | Collector ingest, elephant-flow bandwidth alerts, DDoS accounting |
| **IPFIX (v10)** | `ipfix` | `UDP 4739` | Both | Multi-VRF `domainid` exports, 64-bit packet/octet counters |
| **sFlow v5** | `sflow` | `UDP 6343` | Both | Switch ASIC packet-sampling pipelines over IPv4 and IPv6 |

> **Looking for SNMP, SSH, Telnet, TFTP, FTP, or WHOIS?**
> `snmp1`, `snmp2`, and encrypted `snmp3` live in [**SNMPv1, SNMPv2c & Encrypted SNMPv3 (`l7_snmp.md`)**](l7_snmp.md). Remote CLI (`ssh`, `telnet`), file transfer (`tftp`, `ftp`), and `whois` live in [**Layer 7 — Web, Cloud, Transport Security, VoIP & Remote Access (`l7_web_and_cloud.md`)**](l7_web_and_cloud.md).

## Infrastructure and Telemetry Testing Use Cases

### 1. Test DNS Sinkholes, TCP Zone Transfers (AXFR) & Rogue `dhcp` Without Poisoning Your Lab
Plugging a rogue DHCP server into an access switch just to verify DHCP snooping is a great way to accidentally blackhole the office subnet, and editing `bind` zones for a single **Suricata** AXFR test gets old fast. Script dual-stack `dhcp` DORA/SARR leases, sinkholed `dns` replies, TCP AXFR transfers, and `mdns` multicast announcements offline:

```frameassembly
host client_v4 { ip 192.168.20.100 mac 00:50:56:20:00:64 }
host infra_v4  { ip 192.168.20.1   mac 00:50:56:20:00:01 }
host client_v6 { ip 2001:db8:20::100 mac 00:50:56:62:00:64 }
host infra_v6  { ip 2001:db8:20::1   mac 00:50:56:62:00:01 }

flow ddi_and_onboarding_v4(c, s) {
    // 1. Full DHCPv4 DORA lease negotiation (auto-routes UDP 68 <-> 67)
    c -> s dhcp discover xid 0x10203040 chaddr 00:50:56:20:00:64 hostname "eng-ws-01" wait 2ms
    c <- s dhcp offer xid 0x10203040 yiaddr 192.168.20.100 siaddr 192.168.20.1 chaddr 00:50:56:20:00:64 subnetmask 255.255.255.0 router 192.168.20.1 dnsserver 192.168.20.1 leasetime 86400 wait 2ms
    c -> s dhcp request xid 0x10203040 ciaddr 192.168.20.100 yiaddr 192.168.20.100 chaddr 00:50:56:20:00:64 hostname "eng-ws-01" wait 2ms
    c <- s dhcp ack xid 0x10203040 yiaddr 192.168.20.100 siaddr 192.168.20.1 chaddr 00:50:56:20:00:64 subnetmask 255.255.255.0 router 192.168.20.1 dnsserver 192.168.20.1 leasetime 86400 wait 5ms

    // 2. Normal DNS A lookup (RCODE 0) + sinkholed C2 lookup (RCODE 3 = NXDOMAIN)
    c -> s dns query txid 1010 qname "git.corp.example.com" qtype "a" wait 1ms
    c <- s dns response txid 1010 qname "git.corp.example.com" qtype "a" rdata "192.168.20.55" rcode 0 ansttl 300 wait 2ms
    c -> s dns query txid 1011 qname "ransom-beacon.bad.example" qtype "a" wait 1ms
    c <- s dns response txid 1011 qname "ransom-beacon.bad.example" qtype "a" rcode 3 wait 2ms

    // 3. Unauthorized DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR) over TCP 53 (auto-prepends 2-byte RFC 1035 length)
    c -> s tcp syn srcport 53100 dstport 53 win 64240 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    c <- s tcp syn ack win 65535 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    c -> s tcp ack wait 1ms
    c -> s transport tcp dns query txid 1012 qname "corp.example.com" qtype "axfr" wait 2ms

    // 4. Apple Bonjour / Avahi mDNS printer discovery (auto-targets 224.0.0.251 / 01:00:5e:00:00:fb)
    c -> s mdns query txid 0 qname "_ipp._tcp.local" qtype "ptr" wait 2ms
    c <- s mdns response txid 0 qname "_ipp._tcp.local" qtype "ptr" rdata "floor3-printer._ipp._tcp.local" ansttl 120
}

flow ddi_and_onboarding_v6(c6, s6) {
    // DHCPv6 SARR (auto-routes UDP 546 <-> 547) + IPv6 AAAA lookup + mDNS to ff02::fb
    c6 -> s6 dhcp solicit xid 0xabcdef chaddr 00:50:56:62:00:64 wait 2ms
    c6 <- s6 dhcp advertise xid 0xabcdef chaddr 00:50:56:62:00:64 wait 2ms
    c6 -> s6 dhcp request xid 0xabcdef chaddr 00:50:56:62:00:64 wait 2ms
    c6 <- s6 dhcp reply xid 0xabcdef chaddr 00:50:56:62:00:64 wait 5ms
    c6 -> s6 dns query txid 2020 qname "git.corp.example.com" qtype "aaaa" wait 1ms
    c6 <- s6 dns response txid 2020 qname "git.corp.example.com" qtype "aaaa" rdata "2001:db8:20::55" ansttl 300 wait 2ms
    c6 -> s6 mdns query txid 0 qname "_ssh._tcp.local" qtype "ptr"
}

compile {
    ddi_and_onboarding_v4(client_v4, infra_v4)
    ddi_and_onboarding_v6(client_v6, infra_v6)
}
```

### 2. Verify IEEE 1588v2 `ptp` Grandmaster Queues & `ntp` Kiss-o'-Death Handling Without Hardware Clocks
Hardware IEEE 1588v2 Grandmaster clocks cost thousands of dollars, which is painful when you just want to check that your switches put `ptp` Event (`UDP 319`) and General (`UDP 320`) packets into the `dscp 46` (EF) strict-priority queue or test how clients react to a Stratum-0 `ntp` Kiss-o'-Death (`"RATE"`):

```frameassembly
host grandmaster { ip 10.158.0.1  mac 00:1c:73:00:01:01 }
host boundary_sw { ip 10.158.0.50 mac 00:1c:73:00:01:50 }

flow precision_timing_audit(gm, sw) {
    // 1. Stratum-1 GPS NTP sync + Stratum-0 Kiss-o'-Death ("RATE") throttling response
    sw -> gm dscp 46 ntp li 0 vn 4 mode 3 stratum 2 poll 6 precision -18 refid "INIT" txtimestamp 0xe9b0000100000000 wait 1ms
    sw <- gm dscp 46 ntp li 0 vn 4 mode 4 stratum 1 poll 6 precision -24 refid "GPS"  txtimestamp 0xe9b0000100001000 wait 5ms
    sw <- gm dscp 46 ntp li 3 vn 4 mode 4 stratum 0 poll 6 precision -24 refid "RATE" txtimestamp 0xe9b0000200000000 wait 5ms

    // 2. IEEE 1588v2 two-step PTP cycle (auto-routes sync/delayreq -> 319, announce/followup/delayresp -> 320)
    gm -> sw vlan 158 pcp 5 dscp 46 ptp announce  domain 24 seqid 500 clockid "GM-CLK01" wait 500us
    gm -> sw vlan 158 pcp 5 dscp 46 ptp sync      domain 24 seqid 501 clockid "GM-CLK01" wait 100us
    gm -> sw vlan 158 pcp 5 dscp 46 ptp followup  domain 24 seqid 501 clockid "GM-CLK01" wait 200us
    sw -> gm vlan 158 pcp 5 dscp 46 ptp delayreq  domain 24 seqid 501 clockid "SW-CLK50" wait 200us
    gm -> sw vlan 158 pcp 5 dscp 46 ptp delayresp domain 24 seqid 501 clockid "GM-CLK01"
}

compile { precision_timing_audit(grandmaster, boundary_sw) }
```

### 3. Audit 802.1X `radius` Policies & `tacacs` CLI Blocks Without Touching Jump Boxes
Testing NAC policies or SIEM alerts for unauthorized router `reload` commands normally forces you to wrestle supplicant certificates or type dangerous commands on a live jump box. Here you can script `radius` auth (`UDP 1812`), accounting (`UDP 1813`), and TACACS+ (`tacacs`) command auditing (`TCP 49`) directly:

```frameassembly
host access_sw  { ip 10.60.1.10  mac 00:50:56:60:00:10 }
host aaa_server { ip 10.60.1.200 mac 00:50:56:60:02:00 }
host sw_v6      { ip 2001:db8:60::10 }
host aaa_v6     { ip 2001:db8:60::200 }

flow nac_and_cli_audit(nas, aaa) {
    // 1. RADIUS 802.1X MFA challenge -> Accept (UDP 1812) -> Accounting Start (auto-switches to UDP 1813)
    nas -> aaa radius accessrequest id 10 user "alice@corp.example" nasip 10.60.1.10 servicetype 2 wait 2ms
    nas <- aaa radius accesschallenge id 10 user "alice@corp.example" wait 2ms
    nas -> aaa radius accessrequest id 11 user "alice@corp.example" nasip 10.60.1.10 servicetype 2 wait 2ms
    nas <- aaa radius accessaccept id 11 user "alice@corp.example" framedip 10.60.20.55 servicetype 2 wait 5ms
    nas -> aaa radius accountingrequest id 12 user "alice@corp.example" nasip 10.60.1.10 framedip 10.60.20.55 wait 2ms
    nas <- aaa radius accountingresponse id 12 wait 5ms

    // 2. TACACS+ login, privilege-15 command authorization, and reload accounting over TCP 49
    nas -> aaa tcp syn srcport 51049 dstport 49 win 64240 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    nas <- aaa tcp syn ack win 65535 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    nas -> aaa tcp ack wait 1ms
    nas -> aaa tacacs authen seq 1 flags 1 sessionid 900101 user "netadmin" data "tty0" wait 2ms
    nas <- aaa tacacs authen seq 2 flags 1 sessionid 900101 user "netadmin" data "PASS" wait 2ms
    nas -> aaa tacacs author seq 1 flags 1 sessionid 900102 user "netadmin" data "cmd=configure;cmd-arg=terminal" wait 2ms
    nas <- aaa tacacs author seq 2 flags 1 sessionid 900102 user "netadmin" payload "AUTHOR_STATUS_PASS_ADD" wait 2ms
    nas -> aaa tacacs acct   seq 1 flags 1 sessionid 900103 user "netadmin" data "task_id=42;service=shell;cmd=reload"
}

flow radius_ipv6_avps(nas6, aaa6) {
    // Automatically encodes RFC 3162 NAS-IPv6-Address (95) and RFC 6911 Framed-IPv6-Address (168)
    nas6 -> aaa6 radius accessrequest id 20 user "bob@corp.example" nasip 2001:db8:60::10 servicetype 2 wait 2ms
    nas6 <- aaa6 radius accessaccept  id 20 user "bob@corp.example" framedip 2001:db8:60:20::55
}

compile {
    nac_and_cli_audit(access_sw, aaa_server)
    radius_ipv6_avps(sw_v6, aaa_v6)
}
```

### 4. Benchmark SIEM Grok Parsers & Flow Collectors (`syslog`, `netflow`, `ipfix`, `sflow`) on Demand
Waiting for a hardware router's active flow timeout or generating 20 GB of synthetic traffic on a laptop just to test **ElastiFlow**, **Akvorado**, `pmacct`, `nfcapd`, or **Splunk** alerts is a waste of an afternoon. Declare the exact byte/packet counters and syslog fields in four lines:

```frameassembly
host core_exporter { ip 10.250.10.1   mac 00:50:56:fa:00:01 }
host telemetry_col { ip 10.250.10.100 mac 00:50:56:fa:01:00 }
host leaf_v6       { ip 2001:db8:fa::1 }
host collector_v6  { ip 2001:db8:fa::100 }

flow observability_ingest(rtr, col) {
    // 1. UDP 514 Syslog warning (PRI 132) + reliable TCP 514 SSH security audit log
    rtr -> col syslog facility 16 severity 4 hostname "core-rtr-01" app "bgpd" procid "1842" msgid "BGP-4-MAXPFX" msg "Neighbor 198.51.100.1 prefix count 85000 exceeds 80% threshold" wait 1ms
    rtr -> col tcp syn srcport 51514 dstport 514 win 65535 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    rtr <- col tcp syn ack win 65535 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    rtr -> col tcp ack wait 1ms
    rtr -> col transport tcp syslog facility 10 severity 5 hostname "core-rtr-01" app "sshd" procid "4410" msgid "SEC_LOGIN" msg "Accepted publickey for netadmin from 10.254.0.10 port 54122 ssh2" wait 2ms

    // 2. NetFlow v5 (UDP 2055), IPFIX v10 (UDP 4739), and sFlow v5 (UDP 6343) elephant-flow exports
    rtr -> col netflow srcip 198.51.100.25 dstip 203.0.113.80 srcport 51200 proto 6 packets 154000 octets 215600000 wait 1ms
    rtr -> col ipfix domainid 4001 srcip 198.51.100.25 dstip 203.0.113.80 srcport 51200 proto 6 packets 154000 octets 215600000 wait 1ms
    rtr -> col sflow agentip 10.250.10.1 subagentid 1 seq 105 uptime 86400000 samples 1
}

flow ipv6_telemetry(sw6, col6) {
    sw6 -> col6 syslog facility 23 severity 2 hostname "leaf-sw-v6" app "envmon" msgid "FAN-2-FAIL" msg "Tray 2 Fan 1 RPM below critical threshold" wait 1ms
    sw6 -> col6 sflow agentip 2001:db8:fa::1 subagentid 2 seq 500 uptime 172800000 samples 1
}

compile {
    observability_ingest(core_exporter, telemetry_col)
    ipv6_telemetry(leaf_v6, collector_v6)
}
```

## What FrameAssembly Handles for You

* **Message-Aware UDP Port & Multicast Routing:** `dhcp` flips between `68 <-> 67` (IPv4) and `546 <-> 547` (IPv6); `ptp` routes Event messages (`sync`, `delayreq`) to `UDP 319` and General messages (`announce`, `followup`, `delayresp`) to `UDP 320`; `radius` routes Auth to `UDP 1812` and Accounting to `UDP 1813`; `mdns` targets `224.0.0.251` (`01:00:5e:00:00:fb`) or `ff02::fb` (`33:33:00:00:00:fb`) automatically.
* **RFC-Compliant DNS Compression & TCP Framing:** `dns` encodes length-prefixed labels, compresses Answer names (`0xC00C`), and prepends the mandatory 2-byte big-endian message length header whenever `transport tcp` is added.
* **Zero-Math Headers & Identities:** `syslog` computes `<PRI>` from `(facility * 8) + severity`, `ptp` derives an IEEE EUI-64 `ClockIdentity` from the sender's MAC when `clockid` is omitted, and `dhcp` inherits the sender's MAC into `chaddr` / Option 1 DUID-LL.
* **Dual-Stack Telemetry & AAA Attributes:** `radius` switches `nasip` and `framedip` from IPv4 AVPs (`4` / `8`) to IPv6 AVPs (`95` / `168`) on IPv6 flows, and `sflow` sets `address_type` `1` (IPv4) or `2` (IPv6) automatically.

## Infrastructure & Telemetry Protocol Reference

### 1. Naming, Service Discovery and DHCP (`dns`, `mdns`, `dhcp`)

| Protocol | Flags / Types | Key Modifiers | Wire Behavior & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`dns`** | `query` (default), `response` | `txid <u16>`, `qname "<domain>"`, `qtype "<type>"`, `rdata "<val>"`, `rcode <0..15>`, `ansttl <u32>`, `transport tcp` | `qtype`: `"a"`, `"aaaa"`, `"cname"`, `"ns"`, `"ptr"`, `"mx"`, `"txt"`, `"soa"`, `"srv"`, `"axfr"`, `"any"`; `rcode`: `0` NOERROR, `2` SERVFAIL, `3` NXDOMAIN, `5` REFUSED |
| **`mdns`** | `query` (default), `response` | Same modifiers as `dns` (`txid`, `qname`, `qtype`, `rdata`, `rcode`, `ansttl`) | `UDP 5353`; auto-targets `224.0.0.251` (IPv4) or `ff02::fb` (IPv6) with RFC multicast MACs |
| **`dhcp`** | v4: `discover`, `offer`, `request`, `ack`, `release`; v6: `solicit`, `advertise`, `request`, `reply`, `release` | `xid <u32>`, `chaddr <mac>`, `ciaddr <ipv4>`, `yiaddr <ipv4>`, `siaddr <ipv4>`, `subnetmask <ipv4>`, `router <ipv4>`, `dnsserver <ipv4>`, `hostname "<str>"`, `leasetime <u32>` | Builds 236B BOOTP + `0x63825363` cookie + TLV options on IPv4 (`68/67`) or RFC 8415 DHCPv6 + Option 1 DUID-LL on IPv6 (`546/547`) |

> **Quick Syntax Check (`dns` & `dhcp`):** `query` and `response` are standalone flags—always pass the domain name via `qname "<domain>"` (never `dns query "example.com"`). On `dhcp`, use `xid <u32>` to set the BOOTP / DHCPv6 Transaction ID.

### 2. Clock Sync and Precision Timing (`ntp`, `ptp`)

| Protocol | Sub-Keywords / Modes | Modifiers | Wire Notes & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`ntp`** | `mode <0..7>` (`3` Client default, `4` Server, `5` Broadcast) | `li <0..3>`, `vn <1..4>`, `stratum <0..16>`, `poll <u8>`, `precision <i8>`, `refid "<4char>"`, `txtimestamp <u64>` | 48-byte RFC 5905 frame on `UDP 123`; `stratum 0` = Kiss-o'-Death (`"RATE"`), `1` = Primary (`"GPS"`, `"PPS"`) |
| **`ptp`** | `sync` (default), `delayreq`, `followup`, `delayresp`, `announce` (or `msgtype "<type>"`) | `domain <0..255>`, `seqid <u16>`, `clockid "<8char>"` | 44-byte IEEE 1588v2 frame; `UDP 319` (`sync`, `delayreq`) vs. `UDP 320` (`followup`, `delayresp`, `announce`) |

### 3. AAA Access and CLI Auditing (`radius`, `tacacs`)

| Protocol | Packet Types | Modifiers | Wire Notes & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`radius`** | `accessrequest` (default), `accessaccept`, `accessreject`, `accesschallenge`, `accountingrequest`, `accountingresponse` (or `code "<name>"`) | `id <u8>`, `user "<str>"`, `nasip <ip>`, `servicetype <u32>`, `framedip <ip>` | `UDP 1812` (Auth) / `UDP 1813` (Acct); `servicetype`: `1` Login, `2` Framed/802.1X, `6` Admin |
| **`tacacs`** | `authen` (default), `author`, `acct` (or `type <authen\|author\|acct>`) | `seq <u8>`, `flags <u8>`, `sessionid <u32>`, `user "<str>"`, `data "<str>"`, `payload "<str>"` | `TCP 49`; `flags` defaults to `0x01` (unencrypted) so Wireshark dissects CLI commands |

### 4. Logging and Flow Telemetry (`syslog`, `netflow`, `ipfix`, `sflow`)

| Protocol | Modifiers | Default Port & Wire Behavior |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`syslog`** | `facility <0..23>`, `severity <0..7>`, `pri <0..191>`, `hostname "<str>"`, `app "<str>"`, `procid "<str>"`, `msgid "<str>"`, `msg "<str>"`, `transport tcp` | `UDP 514` (or `TCP 514` with `transport tcp`); RFC 5424 record with `PRI = (facility * 8) + severity` |
| **`netflow`**| `srcip <ip>`, `dstip <ip>`, `srcport <u16>`, `dstport <u16>`, `proto <u8>`, `packets <u32>`, `octets <u32>` | `UDP 2055`; 72-byte Cisco NetFlow v5 header + flow record (`proto`: `1` ICMP, `6` TCP, `17` UDP) |
| **`ipfix`** | `domainid <u32>`, `srcip <ip>`, `dstip <ip>`, `srcport <u16>`, `dstport <u16>`, `proto <u8>`, `packets <u32>`, `octets <u32>` | `UDP 4739`; RFC 7011 IPFIX v10 header + Data Set `256` with 64-bit packet/octet counters |
| **`sflow`** | `agentip <ip>`, `subagentid <u32>`, `seq <u32>`, `uptime <u32>`, `samples <u32>` | `UDP 6343`; dual-stack sFlow v5 header + 32-byte Format `1` Flow Sample record |

#### Handy RFC 5424 `syslog` Severity & Facility Codes

| `severity` | Level | Meaning | Common `facility` | Subsystem |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| `0` / `1` | `emerg` / `alert` | System unusable / immediate action | `0` / `1` / `3` | `kern` / `user` (default) / `daemon` |
| `2` / `3` | `crit` / `err` | Hardware fault / operational error | `4` / `10` | `auth` / `authpriv` (security & logins) |
| `4` / `5` | `warning` / `notice` | Threshold crossed / config or ACL event | `16`..`19` | `local0`..`local3` (router & switch NOS) |
| `6` / `7` | `info` / `debug` | Routine message (`6` default) / trace | `20`..`23` | `local4`..`local7` (firewalls, VPN, audit) |

## Inspecting, Reversing and Replaying Infrastructure Captures

```console
# Extract DNS queries/rcodes, Syslog messages, and IPFIX byte counters in tshark
$ tshark -r infra_check.pcap -T fields -e frame.number -e dns.qry.name -e dns.flags.rcode -e syslog.msg -e cflow.octets64

# Reverse an existing DNS, DHCP, RADIUS, Syslog, or NetFlow/IPFIX capture into .fasm code
$ frameassembly reverse infra_check.pcap edited_infra.fasm

# Test Suricata rules against DNS sinkholes, rogue DHCP, or AXFR zone transfers
$ suricata -r ddi_and_onboarding.pcap -k none

# Replay syslog and flow exports into a live SIEM or collector interface
$ sudo tcpreplay -i eth0 observability_ingest.pcap
```

# Layer 7 — Web, Cloud, Transport Security, VoIP & Remote Access (`docs/l7_web_and_cloud.md`)

[**Use Cases**](#web-cloud-security-and-voip-use-cases) • [**How It Works**](#what-frameassembly-handles-for-you) • [**Web, HTTP/2, gRPC & WebSocket**](#1-web-apis-and-microservices-http-http2-grpc-websocket) • [**TLS & QUIC**](#2-transport-security-and-http3-tls-quic) • [**SSH, Telnet, FTP, TFTP & WHOIS**](#3-remote-access-file-transfer-and-whois-ssh-telnet-tftp-ftp-whois) • [**VoIP, Media & UPnP**](#4-voip-streaming-media-and-upnp-sip-rtp-rtsp-stun-ssdp) • [**Inspect & Replay**](#inspecting-and-replaying-web-and-voip-captures)

## Why Use FrameAssembly for Web, Security & VoIP?

Testing a Web Application Firewall (WAF), checking whether an egress proxy blocks unauthorized TLS 1.3 `SNI`s or UDP `443` `quic`, debugging a broken firewall SIP ALG, or verifying that your SOC wakes up when someone opens Telnet on a management VLAN usually requires way too much throwaway infrastructure -> spin up Docker containers, Nginx reverse proxies, self-signed OpenSSL CAs, `protoc` gRPC stubs, Asterisk PBXs, or `telnetd` on a core switch :)

With **FrameAssembly**, you script both the client request and server response in a few lines of `.fasm` packet code, let the compiler handle TCP `SEQ`/`ACK` math, reply-port swapping, and `Content-Length` headers automatically, and feed the `.pcap` straight into **`tcpreplay`**, **Wireshark** / **`tshark`**, **Suricata**, or **Zeek**:

```frameassembly
host scanner { ip 198.51.100.42 mac 00:0c:29:11:22:33 }
host waf_gw  { ip 203.0.113.10  mac 00:1b:21:aa:bb:cc }

flow waf_and_sni_check(c, gw) {
    // Tracked TCP handshake -> suspicious HTTP POST -> 403 Forbidden WAF block
    c -> gw tcp syn srcport 53080 dstport 80 win 65535 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    c <- gw tcp syn ack win 65535 mss 1460 wait 1ms
    c -> gw tcp ack wait 1ms
    c -> gw http post uri "/api/login" hosthdr "portal.example.com" contenttype "application/json" body "{\"user\":\"admin' OR 1=1--\"}" wait 2ms
    c <- gw http status 403 reason "Forbidden" contenttype "application/json" body "{\"blocked\":\"sqli_rule_942100\"}"
}

compile { waf_and_sni_check(scanner, waf_gw) }
```

```console
$ frameassembly show waf_check.fasm
$ frameassembly waf_check.fasm waf_check.pcap && suricata -r waf_check.pcap -k none
```

| Protocol | Keyword | Default Port | Standard / RFC | Primary Testing Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **HTTP/1.1** | `http` | `TCP 80` | RFC 9110 / 9112 | WAF SQLi/XSS rules, reverse-proxy `X-Forwarded-For` headers, REST status codes |
| **HTTP/2** | `http2` | `TCP 443` | RFC 9113 | Binary stream multiplexing, `SETTINGS` / `WINDOW_UPDATE`, graceful `GOAWAY` |
| **gRPC** | `grpc` | `TCP 50051` | gRPC over HTTP/2 | Service-mesh telemetry, Protobuf RPC paths, `grpc-status` error handling |
| **WebSocket** | `websocket`| `TCP 80` | RFC 6455 | XOR-masked client frames, `PING`/`PONG` keepalives, proxy upgrade policies |
| **TLS 1.2 / 1.3**| `tls` | `TCP 443` | RFC 8446 / 6066 | Firewall `SNI` & `ALPN` inspection, cipher-suite audits, fatal `Alert` drops |
| **QUIC / HTTP/3**| `quic` | `UDP 443` | RFC 9000 / 9114 | UDP `443` firewall pinholes, `Retry` token validation, `0-RTT` & `Short` frames |
| **SSH-2** | `ssh` | `TCP 22` | RFC 4253 | Outdated banner detection (`OpenSSH_7.2`), `KEXINIT` cookies, bastion ACLs |
| **Telnet** | `telnet` | `TCP 23` | RFC 854 / 855 | Cleartext management VLAN IDS alerts, `IAC` (`DO`/`WILL`) option negotiation |
| **TFTP** | `tftp` | `UDP 69` | RFC 1350 | Switch Zero-Touch Provisioning (ZTP), PXE boot blocks, `File not found` errors |
| **FTP** | `ftp` | `TCP 21` | RFC 959 / 2428 | Firewall `PASV`/`EPSV` ALG dynamic pinholes, cleartext credential alerts |
| **WHOIS** | `whois` | `TCP 43` | RFC 3912 | Air-gapped SOC domain/ASN enrichment tests without public RIR rate limits |
| **SIP** | `sip` | `UDP/TCP 5060`| RFC 3261 / 4566 | SBC call signaling (`INVITE`/`200`/`BYE`), SIP ALG mangling, SDP bodies |
| **RTP** | `rtp` | `UDP 5004` | RFC 3550 / 3551 | `DSCP EF` (`46`) voice/video priority queues, jitter & sequence-gap checks |
| **RTSP** | `rtsp` | `TCP 554` | RFC 7826 / 2326 | IP camera NVR VLAN ACLs (`DESCRIBE`/`SETUP`/`PLAY`), `Transport:` ports |
| **STUN** | `stun` | `UDP 3478` | RFC 8489 / 5389 | WebRTC ICE NAT traversal, `XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS` reflexive IP discovery |
| **SSDP / UPnP** | `ssdp` | `UDP 1900` | UPnP DA 1.1 / 2.0 | Rogue UPnP media-server sweeps (`239.255.255.250`), IoT VLAN segmentation |

> **Looking for IoT & Message Broker Protocols (`mqtt`, `coap`, `amqp`)?**
> Those three live in [**Layer 7 — Mail, Identity, Storage, Databases & Message Brokers (`l7_mail_auth_storage_db.md`)**](l7_mail_auth_storage_db.md#message-brokers-and-iot-queues-mqtt-coap-amqp).

## Web, Cloud, Security and VoIP Use Cases

### 1. Audit WAF Rules, Microservice `grpc` Failures & Masked `websocket` Streams Without Backend Stubs
Using `curl` only captures traffic if you already have a live backend returning the exact status code, headers, or `grpc-status: 14 UNAVAILABLE` failure you want to test—and naive packet generators forget RFC 6455's mandatory 32-bit client XOR mask on `websocket` frames so proxies drop them immediately. Script the whole microservice tier directly:

```frameassembly
host api_gw  { ip 10.120.1.10 mac 00:1b:21:10:01:0a }
host app_svc { ip 10.120.1.50 mac 00:1b:21:10:01:32 }

flow web_and_microservice_tier(gw, svc) {
    // 1. HTTP/1.1 POST with reverse-proxy headers + 201 Created JSON response
    gw -> svc http post uri "/v1/orders" version "1.1" hosthdr "api.corp.example" useragent "Envoy/1.31" contenttype "application/json" header "X-Request-Id" "req-4092" header "X-Forwarded-For" "198.51.100.7" body "{\"sku\":\"RTR-9000\",\"qty\":2}" wait 1ms
    gw <- svc http version "1.1" status 201 reason "Created" contenttype "application/json" header "X-Request-Id" "req-4092" body "{\"order_id\":8801,\"status\":\"confirmed\"}" wait 2ms

    // 2. Binary HTTP/2 connection preface -> SETTINGS -> Stream 1 request -> graceful GOAWAY drain
    gw -> svc http2 preface wait 1ms
    gw -> svc http2 settings streamid 0 wait 1ms
    gw <- svc http2 settings streamid 0 wait 1ms
    gw -> svc http2 headers streamid 1 payload ":method GET :path /v2/inventory" wait 1ms
    gw <- svc http2 data streamid 1 payload "{\"in_stock\":true}" wait 1ms
    gw <- svc http2 goaway streamid 0 wait 2ms

    // 3. gRPC unary call and UNAVAILABLE (14) service-mesh failure on TCP 50051
    gw -> svc grpc service "inventory.v1.StockService" method "ReserveItems" payload "PROTOBUF_RESERVE_REQ" wait 1ms
    gw <- svc grpc service "inventory.v1.StockService" method "ReserveItems" grpcstatus 14 payload "upstream_reset" wait 2ms

    // 4. RFC 6455 WebSocket XOR-masked client frame, server reply, PING/PONG, and CLOSE
    gw -> svc websocket text finbit 1 maskkey 0x37fa213d payload "{\"subscribe\":\"orders\"}" wait 1ms
    gw <- svc websocket opcode "text" finbit 1 payload "{\"event\":\"SHIPPED\",\"id\":8801}" wait 1ms
    gw -> svc websocket ping finbit 1 maskkey 0x11223344 payload "hb" wait 1ms
    gw <- svc websocket pong finbit 1 payload "hb" wait 1ms
    gw -> svc websocket close finbit 1 maskkey 0x37fa213d hexpayload "03e8"
}

compile { web_and_microservice_tier(api_gw, app_svc) }
```

### 2. Test Firewall `tls` 1.3 `SNI`/`ALPN` Filtering & UDP `443` `quic` Pinholes Without OpenSSL CAs
Next-gen firewalls and egress proxies inspect cleartext `ClientHello` `SNI` and `ALPN` extensions—and often block or throttle UDP `443` `quic` to force HTTP/3 clients back onto TCP. Verify both policies over IPv6 without generating a single X.509 certificate:

```frameassembly
host client_v6   { ip 2001:db8:443::50 }
host cdn_edge_v6 { ip 2001:db8:443::1 }

flow tls13_and_quic_audit(c, s) {
    // 1. Tracked TCP 443 handshake + TLS 1.3 SNI/ALPN negotiation + encrypted AppData + close_notify Alert
    c -> s tcp syn srcport 54443 dstport 443 win 65535 mss 1440 wscale 7 sackperm wait 1ms
    c <- s tcp syn ack win 65535 mss 1440 wscale 7 sackperm wait 1ms
    c -> s tcp ack wait 1ms
    c -> s tls clienthello recordversion 0x0301 handshakeversion 0x0303 sni "edge.cdn.example.com" ciphersuite 4866 alpn "h2" wait 1ms
    c <- s tls serverhello recordversion 0x0303 handshakeversion 0x0303 ciphersuite 4866 alpn "h2" wait 1ms
    c <- s tls certificate recordversion 0x0303 payload "X509_ECDSA_CERT_CHAIN" wait 1ms
    c <- s tls finished recordversion 0x0303 payload "SERVER_VERIFY" wait 1ms
    c -> s tls finished recordversion 0x0303 payload "CLIENT_VERIFY" wait 1ms
    c -> s tls appdata recordversion 0x0303 payload "ENCRYPTED_H2_GET" wait 1ms
    c -> s tls alert recordversion 0x0303 wait 5ms

    // 2. QUIC v1 Initial -> Retry token challenge -> Initial -> 0-RTT -> Handshake -> 1-RTT Short Header
    c -> s quic initial version 1 dcid 0x8394c8f03e515708 scid 0x1122334455667788 pktnum 1 payload "CRYPTO_CH" wait 1ms
    c <- s quic retry   version 1 dcid 0x1122334455667788 scid 0x9988776655443322 token "retry_tok_v1" wait 1ms
    c -> s quic initial version 1 dcid 0x9988776655443322 scid 0x1122334455667788 token "retry_tok_v1" pktnum 2 payload "CRYPTO_CH_RETRY" wait 1ms
    c -> s quic zerortt version 1 dcid 0x9988776655443322 scid 0x1122334455667788 pktnum 3 payload "H3_0RTT_GET" wait 1ms
    c <- s quic handshake version 1 dcid 0x1122334455667788 scid 0x9988776655443322 pktnum 1 payload "CRYPTO_FIN" wait 1ms
    c <- s quic short dcid 0x1122334455667788 pktnum 2 payload "H3_200_OK_DATA"
}

compile { tls13_and_quic_audit(client_v6, cdn_edge_v6) }
```

### 3. Trigger Legacy `telnet`/`ftp` IDS Alerts, Bastion `ssh` Audits & `tftp` ZTP Without `telnetd`
Every SOC claims to alert on cleartext `telnet` logins, `ftp` passwords, and vulnerable `ssh` banners on management VLANs, yet nobody wants to enable `telnetd` or `vsftpd` on real switches just to test the sensor:

```frameassembly
host admin_ws    { ip 10.50.1.100 }
host core_switch { ip 10.50.1.1 }

flow remote_admin_and_ztp(ws, sw) {
    // 1. SSH-2 banner audit, KEXINIT cookie exchange, NEWKEYS, and encrypted channel payload
    ws -> sw ssh banner "SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_7.2p2" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw ssh banner "SSH-2.0-Cisco-2.0" wait 1ms
    ws -> sw ssh kexinit cookie "00112233445566778899aabbccddeeff" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw ssh kexinit cookie "ffeeddccbbaa99887766554433221100" wait 1ms
    ws -> sw ssh newkeys wait 1ms
    ws <- sw ssh newkeys wait 1ms
    ws -> sw ssh msgcode 94 payload "ENCRYPTED_SHOW_RUN" wait 2ms

    // 2. Cleartext Telnet IAC negotiation (Echo=1, SGA=3) and login prompt on TCP 23
    ws -> sw telnet do 1 will 3 wait 1ms
    ws <- sw telnet will 1 do 3 data "User Access Verification\r\nUsername: " wait 1ms
    ws -> sw telnet data "netadmin\r\n" wait 2ms

    // 3. Switch Zero-Touch Provisioning (ZTP) TFTP config pull on UDP 69
    ws -> sw tftp rrq filename "leaf01-startup.cfg" mode "octet" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw tftp data block 1 payload "hostname leaf01\ninterface Eth1/1\n" wait 1ms
    ws -> sw tftp ack block 1 wait 2ms

    // 4. Cleartext FTP login + Extended Passive Mode (EPSV 229) firewall helper check + WHOIS lookup
    ws <- sw ftp code 220 reply "Switch FTP Ready" wait 1ms
    ws -> sw ftp cmd "USER" arg "admin" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw ftp code 331 reply "Password required" wait 1ms
    ws -> sw ftp cmd "PASS" arg "SwitchPass!2026" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw ftp code 230 reply "User logged in" wait 1ms
    ws -> sw ftp cmd "EPSV" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw ftp code 229 reply "Entering Extended Passive Mode (|||62001|)" wait 2ms
    ws -> sw whois query domain "AS65001" wait 1ms
    ws <- sw whois response domain "AS65001" registrar "IANA Private Use ASN"
}

compile { remote_admin_and_ztp(admin_ws, core_switch) }
```

### 4. Debug Broken `sip` ALGs, `dscp` EF `rtp` Voice Queues, `rtsp` Cameras & Rogue `ssdp` UPnP
Troubleshooting one-way VoIP audio across NAT or firewall SIP ALGs usually means digging two desk phones out of a closet or fighting `sipp` XML templates. Build the entire `stun` + `sip` + `rtp` call flow, `rtsp` NVR camera setup, and `ssdp` multicast sweep in one flow:

```frameassembly
host voip_phone { ip 10.80.1.50 }
host sbc_media  { ip 10.80.1.10 }

flow voip_camera_and_upnp(phone, sbc) {
    // 1. STUN NAT binding discovery (XORs reflexive IP with magic cookie 0x2112A442)
    phone -> sbc stun bindingrequest txid 9001 software "Polycom-VVX/6.4" wait 1ms
    phone <- sbc stun bindingresponse txid 9001 xormappedaddr 203.0.113.50 software "Coturn-4.6" wait 2ms

    // 2. DSCP CS3 (24) SIP call setup + DSCP EF (46) G.711 PCMU RTP stream + SIP BYE
    phone -> sbc dscp 24 sip invite uri "sip:1002@pbx.example.com" from "sip:1001@pbx.example.com" to "sip:1002@pbx.example.com" callid "call-7741@10.80.1.50" cseq 1 contact "sip:1001@10.80.1.50" contenttype "application/sdp" body "v=0\r\nm=audio 5004 RTP/AVP 0\r\n" wait 2ms
    phone <- sbc dscp 24 sip status 200 reason "OK" callid "call-7741@10.80.1.50" cseq 1 wait 2ms
    phone -> sbc dscp 24 sip ack uri "sip:1002@pbx.example.com" callid "call-7741@10.80.1.50" cseq 1 wait 1ms
    phone -> sbc dscp 46 rtp pt 0 seq 1001 timestamp 160 ssrc 0x11223344 marker 1 payload "G711_PCMU_FRAME_1" wait 20ms
    phone <- sbc dscp 46 rtp pt 0 seq 5001 timestamp 160 ssrc 0x99887766 marker 1 payload "G711_PCMU_REPLY_1" wait 20ms
    phone -> sbc dscp 24 sip bye uri "sip:1002@pbx.example.com" callid "call-7741@10.80.1.50" cseq 2 wait 2ms
    phone <- sbc dscp 24 sip status 200 reason "OK" callid "call-7741@10.80.1.50" cseq 2 wait 5ms

    // 3. Security camera RTSP stream setup on TCP 554 (uses transporthdr for RTP/AVP ports)
    phone -> sbc rtsp describe uri "rtsp://10.80.1.10:554/cam01/main" cseq 1 wait 1ms
    phone <- sbc rtsp status 200 cseq 1 wait 1ms
    phone -> sbc rtsp setup uri "rtsp://10.80.1.10:554/cam01/main/track1" cseq 2 transporthdr "RTP/AVP;unicast;client_port=5004-5005" wait 1ms
    phone <- sbc rtsp status 200 cseq 2 session "cam-sess-991" wait 1ms
    phone -> sbc rtsp play uri "rtsp://10.80.1.10:554/cam01/main" cseq 3 session "cam-sess-991" wait 2ms
    phone -> sbc rtsp teardown uri "rtsp://10.80.1.10:554/cam01/main" cseq 4 session "cam-sess-991" wait 2ms

    // 4. SSDP UPnP multicast M-SEARCH and NOTIFY alive advertisement on UDP 1900
    phone -> sbc ssdp msearch hosthdr "239.255.255.250:1900" man "\"ssdp:discover\"" mx 3 st "urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaServer:1" wait 1ms
    phone <- sbc ssdp notify  hosthdr "239.255.255.250:1900" nt "urn:schemas-upnp-org:device:MediaServer:1" nts "ssdp:alive" usn "uuid:media-01::upnp:rootdevice" location "http://10.80.1.10:8200/rootDesc.xml"
}

compile { voip_camera_and_upnp(voip_phone, sbc_media) }
```

## What FrameAssembly Handles for You

* **Shared 4-Tuple TCP State & Port Flipping:** Every TCP-based Layer 7 line (`http`, `http2`, `grpc`, `websocket`, `tls`, `ssh`, `telnet`, `ftp`, `whois`, `rtsp`, or `sip` with `transport tcp`) emits a `PSH ACK` segment, flips ports on `<-` replies, and advances TCP `SEQ`/`ACK` counters by the exact generated payload length.
* **Automatic `Content-Length` & Payload Masking:** Attaching `body "<text>"` to `http` or `sip` computes and inserts the exact `Content-Length` header automatically, while `websocket` XOR-masks payloads with `maskkey` per RFC 6455.
* **Zero-Math Binary Headers:** `http2` packs the 9-byte RFC 9113 frame header, `grpc` writes the 5-byte Protobuf length prefix, `tls` encodes 5-byte Record + 4-byte Handshake lengths plus `SNI`/`ALPN` extensions, `quic` encodes RFC 9000 variable-length payload integers, and `ssh` pads binary packets to 8-byte cipher boundaries.
* **Collision-Free Header Keywords:** Because `host` declares endpoints and `transport tcp|udp` switches Layer 4 protocols, `http`/`ssdp` use `hosthdr` for `Host:` and `rtsp` uses `transporthdr` for `Transport:`.

## Web, Security, Remote Access & VoIP Reference

### 1. Web, APIs and Microservices (`http`, `http2`, `grpc`, `websocket`)

| Protocol | Operations / Frame Types | Modifiers | Wire Notes & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`http`** | `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `head`, `options`, `patch` (or `method "<verb>"`) | `uri "<path>"`, `version "<ver>"`, `hosthdr "<host>"`, `useragent "<ua>"`, `contenttype "<mime>"`, `header "<K>" "<V>"`, `status <100..599>`, `reason "<str>"`, `body "<str>"` | `TCP 80`; setting `status` emits a response, omitting it emits a request; `header` may be repeated |
| **`http2`** | `preface`, `settings` (default), `headers`, `data`, `windowupdate`, `ping`, `goaway` | `streamid <u32>`, `payload "<str>"`, `hexpayload "<hex>"` | `TCP 443`; `preface` emits the 24B `PRI * HTTP/2.0...` string; `streamid 0` = connection control, odd `1, 3, 5` = client streams |
| **`grpc`** | Unary / streaming RPC frame | `service "<pkg.Svc>"`, `method "<Rpc>"`, `grpcstatus <0..16>`, `payload "<str>"` | `TCP 50051`; `grpcstatus`: `0` OK, `3` INVALID_ARGUMENT, `4` DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, `7` PERMISSION_DENIED, `14` UNAVAILABLE, `16` UNAUTHENTICATED |
| **`websocket`**| `text` (default), `binary`, `ping`, `pong`, `close` (or `opcode "<text\|binary\|ping\|pong\|close>"`) | `finbit <0\|1>`, `maskkey <u32>`, `payload "<str>"`, `hexpayload "<hex>"` | `TCP 80`; sets `MASK` bit (`0x80`) and XOR-masks payload bytes with 4-byte `maskkey` |

### 2. Transport Security and HTTP/3 (`tls`, `quic`)

| Protocol | Packet / Record Types | Modifiers | Wire Notes & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`tls`** | `clienthello` (default), `serverhello`, `certificate`, `finished`, `appdata`, `alert` | `recordversion <u16>`, `handshakeversion <u16>`, `sni "<host>"`, `ciphersuite <u16>`, `alpn "<proto>"`, `payload "<str>"` | `TCP 443`; `ciphersuite`: `4865` (`0x1301` AES_128_GCM), `4866` (`0x1302` AES_256_GCM), `4867` (`0x1303` CHACHA20); `alert` defaults to fatal `handshake_failure` (`[2, 40]`) |
| **`quic`** | `initial` (default), `zerortt`, `handshake`, `retry`, `short` | `version <u32>`, `dcid <u64>`, `scid <u64>`, `token "<str>"`, `pktnum <u32>`, `payload "<str>"` | `UDP 443`; `version 1` = RFC 9000 QUIC v1, `0x6b3343cf` = RFC 9369 QUIC v2 |

### 3. Remote Access, File Transfer and WHOIS (`ssh`, `telnet`, `tftp`, `ftp`, `whois`)

| Protocol | Sub-Keywords / Modes | Modifiers | Wire Notes & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`ssh`** | Version banner (default), `kexinit`, `newkeys` | `banner "<str>"`, `msgcode <0..255>`, `cookie "<32hex_or_str>"`, `payload "<str>"` | `TCP 22`; `msgcode`: `20` KEXINIT, `21` NEWKEYS, `50` UserAuth Req, `90` Channel Open, `94` Channel Data |
| **`telnet`** | `will`, `wont`, `do`, `dont` | `[option] <0..255>`, `data "<str>"`, `payload "<str>"` | `TCP 23`; options: `0` Binary, `1` Echo, `3` Suppress Go Ahead, `24` TermType, `31` NAWS |
| **`tftp`** | `rrq` (default), `wrq`, `data`, `ack`, `error` (or `err`) | `filename "<str>"`, `mode "<octet\|netascii>"`, `block <u16>`, `errcode <u16>`, `errmsg "<str>"`, `payload "<str>"` | `UDP 69`; `errcode`: `1` File not found, `2` Access violation, `3` Disk full, `6` File exists |
| **`ftp`** | Client command or 3-digit reply | `cmd "<verb>"`, `arg "<str>"`, `code <100..599>`, `reply "<str>"` | `TCP 21`; `code`: `220` Ready, `331` Pass req, `230` Logged in, `227` PASV, `229` EPSV, `530` Login incorrect |
| **`whois`** | `query` (default), `response` | `domain "<str>"`, `registrar "<str>"`, `payload "<str>"` | `TCP 43`; `domain` accepts domains, IPv4/IPv6 prefixes, or ASNs (`"AS65001"`) |

### 4. VoIP, Streaming Media and UPnP (`sip`, `rtp`, `rtsp`, `stun`, `ssdp`)

| Protocol | Methods / Types | Modifiers | Wire Notes & Defaults |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`sip`** | `invite` (default), `ack`, `bye`, `cancel`, `register`, `options` (or `method "<verb>"`) | `uri "<sip>"`, `status <100..699>`, `reason "<str>"`, `from "<uri>"`, `to "<uri>"`, `callid "<id>"`, `cseq <u32>`, `via "<str>"`, `contact "<uri>"`, `contenttype "<mime>"`, `body "<sdp>"`, `transport tcp\|udp` | `UDP 5060` default (`TCP 5060` with `transport tcp`) |
| **`rtp`** | Media frame | `pt <0..127>`, `seq <u16>`, `timestamp <u32>`, `ssrc <u32>`, `marker <0\|1>`, `payload "<str>"`, `hexpayload "<hex>"` | `UDP 5004` (override via `srcport`/`dstport`); `pt`: `0` PCMU, `8` PCMA, `9` G.722, `18` G.729, `96..127` dynamic Opus/H.264 |
| **`rtsp`** | `options` (default), `describe`, `setup`, `play`, `teardown` (or `method "<verb>"`) | `uri "<url>"`, `status <100..599>`, `cseq <u32>`, `session "<id>"`, `transporthdr "<spec>"` | `TCP 554`; always use `transporthdr` for the RTSP `Transport:` header |
| **`stun`** | `bindingrequest` (default), `bindingresponse`, `bindingerror` | `txid <u32>`, `xormappedaddr <ip>`, `software "<str>"` | `UDP 3478`; pass a plain IPv4 or IPv6 address to `xormappedaddr` (no `:port`) |
| **`ssdp`** | `msearch` (default), `notify` | `hosthdr "<ip:port>"`, `man "<str>"`, `mx <u8>`, `st "<target>"`, `nt "<type>"`, `nts "<sub_type>"`, `usn "<uuid>"`, `location "<url>"` | `UDP 1900`; `nts`: `"ssdp:alive"`, `"ssdp:byebye"`, `"ssdp:update"` |

## Inspecting and Replaying Web and VoIP Captures

```console
# Extract HTTP URIs, TLS SNI/ALPN extensions, and QUIC connection IDs in tshark
$ tshark -r tls13_and_quic_audit.pcap -T fields -e frame.number -e tls.handshake.extensions_server_name -e tls.handshake.extensions_alpn_str -e quic.dcid

# Verify WAF / Suricata / Zeek detection logs offline
$ suricata -r waf_check.pcap -k none
$ zeek -C -r remote_admin_and_ztp.pcap

# Replay VoIP SIP + DSCP EF RTP streams across a lab SBC or QoS trunk
$ sudo tcpreplay -i eth0 voip_camera_and_upnp.pcap
```
